content.text: Physical Geography of India and Andhra Pradesh: Physiography, Geology, Climate, Drainage, and Soil Profiles

Andhra Pradesh is situated along the south-eastern coast of peninsular India between 12°41' to 19°07' N latitudes and 76°45' to 84°40' E longitudes, bounded by the Bay of Bengal on the east with a coastline of 974 km (second longest in mainland India after Gujarat). Geologically and physiographically, the state reflects an ancient Gondwanaland shield comprised of Archaean peninsular gneisses, the Proterozoic Cuddapah Supergroup, and fertile Quaternary deltas created by the peninsular drainage systems.
1. Major Physiographic Divisions of Andhra Pradesh

content.caption: Physiographic Zones of Andhra Pradesh: Geological Makeup and Topographic Relief
rows: The Coastal Plains (Circar Coast)
Extends 974 km from Srikakulam to Tirupati; width varies from 20 km to 80 km in deltas.
0 – 150 meters above MSL; incorporates alluvial deltas of Godavari and Krishna, along with inter-deltaic Colair (Kolleru) lake depression.
Rich Quaternary alluvium; high agricultural productivity, aquaculture, salt pans; contains strategic deep-water ports (Visakhapatnam, Gangavaram, Kakinada, Krishnapatnam, Ramayapatnam).
The Eastern Ghats (Pruvaghata)
Discontinuous chain running northeast to southwest, bifurcated by Godavari and Krishna gorges.
600 – 1680 meters. Highest peak in AP: Arma Konda (Jindhagada, 1690m) in ASR district; Mahendragiri (1501m) near border; Simhachalam, Ananthagiri hills.
Composed of Archaean granulite facies (Charnockites and Khondalites); karst limestone topography with stalactites and stalagmites at Borra Caves (Gosthani river); rich bauxite deposits.
The Rayalaseema Plateau (Peneplain)
Covers Anantapur, Sri Sathya Sai, YSR Kadapa, Kurnool, Nandyal, and Annamayya districts.
300 – 600 meters above MSL. Nallamala, Velikonda, Palakonda, Seshachalam (first Biosphere Reserve in AP), and Erramala ranges.
Cuddapah Crescent Basin; semi-arid red and black soils, prone to rain-shadow aridity; Gandikota Gorge carved into Cuddapah quartzite by the Pennar River ('Grand Canyon of India').

content.caption: The majestic Gandikota gorge on the Pennar River in YSR Kadapa district, carved through resistant quartzites of the Proterozoic Cuddapah Supergroup, popularly celebrated as the Grand Canyon of India.
content.alt_text: Gandikota canyon gorge on the Pennar River

items: Archaean Gneisses and Schists: Forms the fundamental basement complex across Rayalaseema and upland coastal districts (Dharwar equivalents). Hosts granites, building stones, and iron ores.

The Cuddapah Supergroup (Proterozoic): A crescent-shaped intracratonic basin covering ~44,000 sq km. Comprises unmetamorphosed quartzites, shales, and limestones divided into Papaghni, Chitravati, Nallamalai, and Kistna groups. Rich in barites (Mangampeta—world's largest bedded barytes deposit), limestone (cement grade), asbestos, and uranium (Tummalapalle deposit in YSR Kadapa).
The Kurnool Group: Overlies Cuddapah sediments unconformably; contains Narji limestones, Banganapalle diamond-bearing conglomerates, and Owk shales.
Gondwana Formations: Exposed in the Lower Godavari valley (Pranhita-Godavari graben); rich in bituminous coal seams (Singareni/Chintalapudi sandstone).
Deccan Traps: Basaltic lava flows occurring in parts of West Godavari (Pangidi traps).
Coastal Tertiary & Quaternary Sediments: Encompasses Rajahmundry sandstones, Krishna-Godavari (KG) offshore hydrocarbon basin containing vast conventional and coal bed methane (CBM) reserves.

content.text: 3. Major River Drainage Systems & Multi-Purpose Projects

content.caption: Drainage Basins of Andhra Pradesh: Origin, Tributaries, Deltas, and Dams
rows: Godavari ('Dakshina Ganga')
Originates at Trimbakeshwar (Nasik, MH); enters AP near Kunavaram; forms a gorge at Papikondalu; discharges via Gautami, Vasishta, and Vainateya mouths.
Pranhita, Indravati, Sabari, Sileru, Kinnerasani.
Polavaram Project (Indira Sagar - under construction), Sir Arthur Cotton Barrage (Dowleswaram), Sileru Hydroelectric Project.
Krishna River
Originates at Mahabaleshwar (MH); enters AP in Nandyal/Kurnool; breaches Eastern Ghats into Bay of Bengal through Hamsaladeevi.
Tungabhadra, Ghataprabha, Malaprabha, Bhima, Musi, Munneru, Dindi.
Srisailam Dam (major hydropower project), Nagarjuna Sagar Dam (shared with Telangana), Prakasam Barrage (Vijayawada), Pulichintala Project (K.L. Rao Sagar).
Pennar (Pinakini)
Originates at Nandi Hills (Chikkaballapur, KA); traverses Anantapur, Kadapa, and Nellore into Bay of Bengal near Utukuru.
Chitravati, Papaghni, Cheyyeru, Kundu, Sagileru.
Somasila Project (Nellore district), Gandikota Reservoir, Mylavaram Dam.
Medium & Minor Rivers
East-flowing coastal streams rising in Eastern Ghats.
Vamsadhara, Nagavali, Gosthani, Sarada, Tandava, Yeleru, Swarnamukhi, Gundlakamma.
Gotta Barrage (Vamsadhara), Thotapalli Barrage (Nagavali), Gundlakamma Reservoir.

content.text: 4. Climate Dynamics & Indian Monsoons in Andhra Pradesh

AP exhibits a tropical semi-arid to tropical maritime climate (Köppen classification: Aw and As). The state's climatic profile is shaped by the interaction of both the South-West (SW) and North-East (NE) monsoons:

items: South-West Monsoon (June – September): Accounts for over 65% of the state's total rainfall (~940 mm annual average). Coastal districts receive abundant orographic and cyclonic precipitation; however, western Rayalaseema (Anantapur, Kurnool) falls in the deep rain-shadow of the Western Ghats, receiving less than 550 mm of precipitation, making Anantapur the second driest district in India after Jaisalmer.

North-East (Retreating) Monsoon (October – December): South coastal districts (Nellore, Prakasam, Tirupati, Bapatla) receive significant rainfall (up to 50–60% of their annual quota) from the NE monsoon. Tropical depressions forming in the southern Bay of Bengal frequently intensify into severe cyclonic storms striking coastal AP.

Temperature Patterns: Hottest months are April–May with temperatures exceeding 45°C in interior Palnadu and Vijayawada ('Blazing heat / Mandu Eendalu'); winters are pleasant (18°C–25°C), while hill resorts like Lambasingi ('Kashmir of AP') record near-freezing temperatures due to high elevation inversion.

content.caption: Soil Types in Andhra Pradesh, Agricultural Characteristics, and Regional Spread
rows: Red Soils (Red Loams & Red Sandy - Alfisols)
Formed by weathering of ancient crystalline granites; rich in iron oxides giving red hue; deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic humus; highly porous.
Rayalaseema plateau (Anantapur, Chittoor, Kadapa) and parts of upland coast. Crops: Groundnut, pulses, millets, castor, and oilseeds.
Black Soils (Regur - Vertisols)
Derived from basaltic traps and calcareous rocks; high clay content with montmorillonite; self-ploughing property (deep cracks when dry, sticky when wet); high moisture retention.
Guntur, Palnadu, Prakasam, Kurnool, and Krishna river uplands. Crops: Cotton, chillies, tobacco, sugarcane, and sorghum.
Alluvial Soils (Entisols / Inceptisols)
Deposited along river deltas and coastal tracts by Godavari, Krishna, and Pennar; rich in potash and lime; highly fertile with loamy textures.
East Godavari, Konaseema, West Godavari, Krishna, Bapatla. Crops: Paddy, sugarcane, banana, turmeric, coconut, and vegetables.
Coastal Sandy & Laterite Soils (Ultisols)
Sandy soils line the littoral fringe; laterites occur on hill cappings in Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, and Nellore formed through intense tropical leaching; rich in iron/aluminium bauxites.
Littoral coast and Ghat margins. Crops: Cashew nut, casuarina, coconut, and horticultural plantations.

content.text: Part A: Mains Analytical & Descriptive Questions

items:
Describe the major physiographic divisions of Andhra Pradesh. How does the topographical diversity influence the agricultural patterns of the state? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Delineate the three broad regions: Coastal Plains, Eastern Ghats, and the Rayalaseema Peneplain; explain how fertile Quaternary alluvium in the deltas promotes intensive paddy and sugarcane cultivation; contrast with the semi-arid, rain-shadow Rayalaseema plateau which necessitates drought-resistant dryland farming (groundnut, millets, pulses); highlight the Eastern Ghats' shifting podu cultivation and horticultural crops (coffee in Araku); conclude on the urgent imperative for inter-basin river transfers (Pattiseema, Polavaram) to balance physiographic disparities.

Examine the geological significance of the Cuddapah Basin in Andhra Pradesh with special reference to its mineral resources. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Introduce the crescent-shaped Proterozoic Cuddapah Supergroup (~44,000 sq km); outline stratigraphic divisions (Papaghni, Chitravati, Nallamalai, Kistna); detail key mineral occurrences: world-class bedded barytes deposit at Mangampeta, high-grade cement limestones, asbestos, chrysotile, and the massive Tummalapalle uranium reserves; discuss its economic role in anchoring India's cement and nuclear fuel industrial base.

Analyze the rainfall distribution in Andhra Pradesh with respect to the South-West and North-East monsoons. Why does Rayalaseema experience chronic drought? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Quantify precipitation shares (SW monsoon ~65%, NE monsoon ~35%); explain why Rayalaseema (especially Anantapur) is located in the rain-shadow of the Western Ghats during the SW monsoon; note that it lies too far inland to receive substantial moisture from the NE monsoon; describe resulting arid agro-climatic conditions; discuss mitigation measures like micro-irrigation, farm ponds (Panta Sanjeevani), and canal extensions (Handri-Neeva, Galeru-Nagari).

content.text: Part B: Screening / Prelims Objective Questions

items:
Q1. Which is the highest mountain peak in Andhra Pradesh and the Eastern Ghats?
(a) Mahendragiri
(b) Arma Konda (Jindhagada)
(c) Galikonda
(d) Horsley Hills
Correct Answer: (b) Arma Konda (Jindhagada) [Explanation: Arma Konda (also known as Jindhagada Peak, 1,690 meters), located in the Araku Valley / Alluri Sitharama Raju district, is the highest peak in Andhra Pradesh and the entire Eastern Ghats range.]

Q2. The world's largest known bedded deposit of Barytes (heavy spar) is located at which place in Andhra Pradesh?
(a) Tummalapalle (Kadapa)
(b) Mangampeta (YSR Kadapa)
(c) Banganapalle (Kurnool)
(d) Macherla (Palnadu)
Correct Answer: (b) Mangampeta (YSR Kadapa) [Explanation: Mangampeta in YSR Kadapa district holds the world's largest single bedded deposit of grey bedded barytes, mined extensively by APMDC.]

Q3. The famous Borra Caves in Alluri Sitharama Raju district were formed by the subterranean karstic erosion of limestone by which river?
(a) Vamsadhara
(b) Gosthani
(c) Nagavali
(d) Champavathi
Correct Answer: (b) Gosthani [Explanation: The Gosthani River flows through the limestone deposits of Ananthagiri hills, creating the subterranean karst stalactites and stalagmites of Borra Caves.]

Q4. Which soil type covers the largest geographical area (approximately 65%) in Andhra Pradesh?
(a) Alluvial Soils
(b) Black Regur Soils
(c) Red Soils (Alfisols)
(d) Laterite Soils
Correct Answer: (c) Red Soils (Alfisols) [Explanation: Red soils derived from Archaean granite-gneiss parent rocks occupy approximately 65% of the state's total area, particularly dominant across the Rayalaseema plateau.]

Q5. Which multi-purpose river valley project in Andhra Pradesh was declared a 'National Project' under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014?
(a) Srisailam Project
(b) Veligonda Project
(c) Polavaram (Indira Sagar) Project
(d) Nagarjuna Sagar Project
Correct Answer: (c) Polavaram (Indira Sagar) Project [Explanation: The Polavaram project across the Godavari River was statutorily declared a Project of National Importance under Section 90 of the AP Reorganisation Act 2014.]
